title: Stage 5 (boss): Rotation, audit and export
summary: Version and rotate the key-encryption keys, keep a tamper-evident HMAC-chained audit log, and export the whole vault as one authenticated blob.

steps.title: Stage 5: running it for years
body: A vault that lives for years needs three more things: keys that can be **rotated**, a log nobody can quietly edit, and a **backup** that is safe to keep anywhere.
**Versioned key-encryption keys.** DEKs are no longer wrapped with the master key itself but with a KEK derived from it per version:
```csharp
Kek(master, v) = HKDF.DeriveKey(HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, master, 32, Array.Empty<byte>(), UTF8($"vault-kek-v{v}"))
Each entry records the `Version` that wrapped its DEK (add `int Version` to `Entry`). New entries use the current version, which starts at 1.
| Command | Prints |
| `info <name>` | `<name>: kek v<version>` |
| `rotate` | `rotated to v<n> (<k> entries on older versions)`: new entries now use the new version; old ones stay readable |
| `rewrap` | `rewrapped <k> data keys to v<n>`: every entry not on the current version, ordinal order, a fresh `NextNonce()` each; all-or-nothing like `passwd` |
| `retire v<n>` | `retired v<n>`: that version may never unwrap again |

`rotate`, `rewrap` and `retire` need the vault unlocked (`error: locked`). `retire` refuses, in this order: not `v` + a number from 1 to current (`error: no key version <arg>`), the current one (`error: <arg> is the current version`), one already retired (`error: <arg> is already retired`), one still in use (`error: <arg> still protects <k> entries`). `passwd` rewraps each DEK under the **same version** of the new master's KEK.

steps.prompt: Why does `retire v1` refuse while any entry is still on v1, instead of just deleting the key?
options: Retiring a key that still protects data would make that data unreadable forever; rotation is only finished once everything is rewrapped
Because HKDF cannot derive v1 again
It shouldn't: retiring early is more secure
steps.explain: Rotation has three phases: start using the new key, migrate (rewrap) what the old one protects, then retire it. Skipping the middle phase is how teams lose data.

steps.title: A tamper-evident audit log
body: At `init`, derive an audit key `auditKey = HKDF(master, "vault-audit")` (same `SubKey` shape as the KEKs). It is kept for the life of the vault, even across `passwd` (a real vault would store it wrapped, like a DEK).
Every log line is `"<n> <event>"` (n counts from 1), and its MAC covers the **previous MAC**:
```text
mac[0] = 32 zero bytes
mac[n] = HMACSHA256(auditKey, mac[n-1] + UTF8(line[n]))
Change, insert or reorder any line and its MAC (and every one after it) stops matching. Step through a three-line chain below and watch each MAC feed the next.

Events logged, only on success: `init`, `unlock`, `unlock-failed` (a wrong password, the one failure that is logged), `lock`, `put <name>`, `get <name>`, `share <entry> <user>`, `passwd`, `rotate v<n>`, `rewrap`, `retire v<n>`.

code: string[] lines = { "1 init", "2 put github", "3 get github" };

steps.prompt: An attacker changes line 2 of a three-line chain but cannot recompute MACs. Verification walks the chain from the start, using each *stored* MAC as the next link. What does this print?
code: byte[] Link(byte[] prev, string line) => HMACSHA256.HashData(key, prev.Concat(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(line)).ToArray());
var lines = new List<string> { "1 init", "2 put github", "3 get github" };
foreach (var l in lines) { p = Link(p, l); macs.Add(p); }
steps.explain: The edited line fails. Line 3 still verifies against the *stored* MAC of line 2, so the vault reports the first broken link. Notice what a chain alone cannot catch: deleting the last lines. Real systems also publish or store the latest head somewhere the attacker cannot reach.

steps.title: Versions and the audit chain
prompt: Add key versions (`info`, `rotate`, `rewrap`, `retire`) and the audit log, plus:

| `audit` | every line, then `chain ok (<n> entries, head <first 4 bytes of the last MAC, hex>)`, or the lines then `chain broken at entry <n>` (the first that fails); `error: no vault` before `init` |
| `audit-edit <n> <text>` | `edited entry <n>`, after replacing line n with `"<n> <text>"` and keeping its MAC; `error: no audit entry <n>` if out of range |

ends by printing the log lines `1 init`, `2 put github`, `3 rotate v2`, `4 rewrap`, `5 retire v1`, then `chain ok (5 entries, head <8 hex>)`. The head hex is exact, so it only matches if your audit key, line format and chaining follow the spec. Everything from stages 1 to 4 must keep working.

require.message: Derives versioned KEKs and the audit key with HKDF
Chains the audit log with HMAC-SHA256

hints: One helper for every derived key: `static byte[] SubKey(byte[] master, string label)`; then `Kek(master, v) => SubKey(master, $"vault-kek-v{v}")` and the audit key is `SubKey(master, "vault-audit")`.
Make `Unwrap(byte[] master, string name, Entry e)` derive `Kek(master, e.Version)`, and return `null` for a retired version.
`Log(string evt)`: `line = $"{audit.Count + 1} {evt}"`, previous MAC is 32 zero bytes for the first line, then append `(line, mac)`.

steps.title: One authenticated export
body: Last: back the vault up as **one blob** that is safe to store anywhere.
| Command | Prints |
| `export` | `exported <n> entries`; logs `export` first, so the export contains its own log line |
| `tamper-export` | `export file tampered`, after flipping bit 0 of the byte at `blob.Length / 2` |
| `import <password>` | `imported <n> entries`, then the vault is unlocked and logs `import`; or `error: import failed (wrong password or damaged file)` |
`export` needs the vault unlocked; `tamper-export` and `import` with no export yet print `error: nothing exported`.

The blob is `nonce (12) | ciphertext | tag (16)`, sealed with AES-GCM under `SubKey(master, "vault-export")`, with a nonce from `NextNonce()` and the associated data `"dojo-vault-export-v1"`. Inside: the key-check, the audit key, the counter, the current version, the retired versions, every entry (name, version and all six byte arrays) and the audit log. The byte format is yours; a `BinaryWriter` with length-prefixed arrays is simple and exact.
Two rules make it correct:
- **Verify, then replace.** Decrypt the whole blob first. Only when the tag checks out do you touch the vault, so a wrong password or a flipped bit changes nothing.

- **Never rewind the counter.** An older export carries an older counter. If import simply restored it, the next `put` would reuse nonces already spent under the same KEK. Keep `counter = Math.Max(counter, imported)`.

steps.prompt: After `export`, the owner adds an entry (using nonces 6 and 7), then imports the export, whose saved counter is 5. What goes wrong if import sets `counter = 5`?
options: The next put reuses nonce 7 under the same KEK that already used it: a GCM nonce reuse
Nothing: the new entry has its own random DEK, so every nonce is safe
The import fails its tag check
steps.explain: The *data* nonce is under a fresh DEK, so that one is harmless. But the *wrap* nonce is under the KEK, which is the same before and after the import. Backups, snapshots and VM clones that rewind counters are a classic real-world source of nonce reuse.

steps.title: Export and import
prompt: Add `export`, `tamper-export` and `import` as specified. Everything from stages 1 to 5 must keep working.
error: import failed (wrong password or damaged file)

That finishes the vault: a master key that is never stored, authenticated entries under their own keys, password changes and rotations that touch only small wrapped keys, signed sharing, a log that cannot be silently edited, and a backup that is all-or-nothing.
